title: Crypto volatility, open banking, and Zcash privacy: the compliance trifecta
summary: Bitcoin's near-$87k reversal, Zcash's faster shielded transactions, and open banking's credit-invisible pipeline all land on the same week as overdue HKMA STR quality findings. Alex and Jordan work through what each means for your Monday morning.
script:
JORDAN: I want to put three things on the table that, on the surface, look like technology stories. Bitcoin nearly hitting eighty seven thousand dollars before reversing hard, Zcash activating dramatically faster block times on testnet, and open banking pipelines being used to score credit invisibles. My read is that all three are compliance stories in disguise.

ALEX: I'll take that framing, but I want to resist the idea that they carry equal weight. Because for me, Zcash is the one that should be sitting in a VASP compliance officer's inbox right now, not the Bitcoin price.

JORDAN: Why lead there rather than the volatility story?

ALEX: Because Bitcoin volatility is a known operational stressor. VASPs have built, or should have built, playbooks for price spikes and reversals. What Zcash's testnet activation tells you is something genuinely new. Twenty-five-second block intervals, down from a seventy-five-second target. That is a ninety percent reduction in confirmation friction for shielded transactions. Shielded. The transactions that are already the hardest for transaction monitoring systems to surveil.

JORDAN: And that is precisely my concern, but I'd push back on where the urgency sits. The testnet activation is not mainnet. Compliance teams should be watching it, absolutely. But I worry that flagging testnet activity as an immediate Monday-morning action creates noise that desensitises people to the things that are actually live today.

ALEX: That is a fair distinction. But the lead time between testnet and mainnet on major protocol upgrades has compressed significantly. If your transaction-monitoring vendor has not already mapped its detection logic for Zcash's shielded pool, and your firm is operating in any jurisdiction that permits VASP activity touching privacy coins, this is the moment to have that conversation, not after mainnet.

JORDAN: Agreed on that. So the concrete action here is this. If you are the compliance officer or MLRO at a virtual asset service provider, pull your current ruleset coverage for privacy-coin transactions this week. Check specifically whether your rules distinguish between transparent and shielded Zcash addresses, because many off-the-shelf transaction monitoring configurations do not. Raise it with your technology or vendor team before the end of this week, not when mainnet arrives.

ALEX: On the Bitcoin volatility story, I do not want to dismiss it entirely. Bitcoin briefly touching the equivalent of around eighty seven thousand US dollars before reversing sharply on the fifth of October is operationally significant for one specific reason. Real-time suspicious transaction reporting obligations do not pause for market volatility. In Singapore, MAS Notice 626 requires timely filing. In Australia, section 41 of the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing Act requires prompt reporting. When price swings are that steep, transaction volumes spike, and the gap between automated alert generation and analyst review widens.

JORDAN: Which is a resourcing problem as much as a compliance problem. And I'd be blunter than you about this. If your transaction monitoring team is running at capacity on a calm day, a price event of that magnitude is going to create a queue that your existing headcount cannot clear within your internal SLA. That is a governance risk, not just an operational one.

ALEX: So what do you tell a head of financial crime about that?

JORDAN: I'd say pull your alert-to-review turnaround data from the last major price event and put it in front of your risk committee this week. If the numbers show queue degradation during high-volatility periods, you have a documented gap that needs a remediation plan. Better to surface that proactively than to have a supervisor identify it in an examination.

ALEX: Shifting our focus to the open banking story. The Salad Finance piece is framed as a financial-inclusion story about credit invisibles, the estimated one point seven billion adults globally who sit outside formal credit-scoring systems. But there is a compliance read here that I think practitioners are underweighting.

JORDAN: I think the compliance read is actually the more interesting read. Open banking data pipelines being used for creditworthiness assessment means that lenders are ingesting transaction history, income flows, and behavioral data from third-party sources that were not originally designed as AML inputs. The question for an MLRO is whether your customer due diligence framework has kept pace with your credit team's data sourcing.

ALEX: That is exactly right. And in Singapore, MAS Notice 626's requirements around customer risk profiling assume that the data underpinning that profile is understood and governed. If your credit team is using open banking feeds to approve a customer, and your compliance team is using a separate data set to risk-rate that same customer, you potentially have a coherence problem at the point of onboarding.

JORDAN: And in Australia, AUSTRAC's guidance on the AML and CTF Program, specifically the Part B customer identification obligations under section 84 of the AML/CTF Act, would expect that any novel data source used to identify or assess a customer has been reviewed within the annual program review. Speaking of which, that annual board-level review was due in August. If your board has not signed off the updated program yet, that is overdue.

ALEX: Before we close, I want to flag a still-live obligation for Hong Kong listeners specifically. The HKMA's Q4 2025 STR quality thematic review issued deficiency letters to approximately twenty-five percent of authorised institutions earlier this year. Closure of those findings is the current obligation under the HKMA's Supervisory Policy Manual CG-5.

JORDAN: And the HKMA annual self-assessment return, covering customer due diligence, ongoing monitoring, sanctions screening, STR filing, training, governance, and independent audit under the HKMA AML and CFT Guideline section eleven, had a September thirtieth deadline. If you have not submitted, or if the submission was placeholder pending board sign-off, that needs immediate attention. An overdue self-assessment alongside an open thematic deficiency letter is not a combination you want going into any supervisory engagement.

ALEX: On that STR quality point, the read-across from the HKMA's findings is worth stating clearly. The deficiency letters from the thematic review focused on narrative quality, not just volume. Supervisors are reading your STR text. They are assessing whether the narrative explains the predicate suspicion, links the activity to the customer's risk profile, and documents what was considered and why. A technically-filed STR with a thin narrative is still a finding.

JORDAN: So if you are in scope for that thematic review closure, do not just respond to the letter. Use this as a trigger to run a sample review of the last quarter's STR narratives against the JFIU's quality benchmarks before you respond. Show the supervisor a revised quality framework, not just an acknowledgement.

ALEX: That is a good place to end. Three technology stories that turned out to be compliance stories, and two live obligations that listeners should not be leaving until end of month. The full obligation register and source links for everything discussed today are at amlagents dot streamlit dot app.

JORDAN: And if you are listening to this on a Tuesday morning and any of it felt uncomfortably close to home, that is the point. We'll be back tomorrow.
